metaTitle: Can an LLC Own a C Corp? Structure and Tax Rules
metaDescription: An LLC can own stock in a C corporation, and a C corp can own an LLC. Here is how cross-entity ownership works, tax mechanics, and S-corp restrictions.
h1: Can an LLC Own a C Corp?
subtitle: Cross-entity ownership rules between limited liability companies and corporations, disregarded tax mechanics, and the key shareholder restrictions.
introText:
An LLC can own stock in a C corporation, and a C corporation can own an LLC. Federal law places no restriction on who can hold shares in a C corporation, meaning any legal entity, including a limited liability company (LLC), can be a corporate shareholder. State limited liability company statutes likewise permit corporations to hold membership interests in an LLC, which frequently occurs when a corporation creates a wholly owned subsidiary.

At ModernWallet, we see business founders run into confusion because ownership rules differ sharply between business structures. While an LLC can easily own C corporation stock, that same LLC generally cannot hold shares in an S corporation. Distinguishing between ownership structure, state entity formation, and federal tax classification determines whether your intended corporate setup works under federal tax law.

sections.heading: Can an LLC Own a C Corp? Stock Ownership Rules
sections.body:
A limited liability company (LLC) can legally purchase and hold shares in a C corporation (C corp). The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) impose zero limits on who or what entity may hold shares in a standard C corporation. A C corporation shareholder can be a United States citizen, a foreign national, a trust, an estate, a general partnership, another corporation, or an LLC.

Because state business codes treat an LLC as a distinct legal person capable of acquiring assets, entering contracts, and holding securities, the LLC simply buys or receives corporate shares like any other investor. The C corporation issues share certificates or records book-entry shares directly in the name of the LLC. When the C corporation distributes dividends from after-tax corporate earnings, it issues those dividend checks or wire transfers directly to the LLC.

This ownership setup is common among investment groups, family holding structures, and private corporate groups. Holding C corporation shares inside an LLC allows multiple business partners to manage an equity investment collectively under an operating agreement while maintaining an asset-protection wrapper between the investors and their corporate holdings.

sections.heading: Shareholder Restrictions for S Corporations
sections.body:
While an LLC can freely own stock in a C corporation, an LLC generally cannot own shares in an S corporation (S corp). Federal tax rules governing S corporations establish strict eligibility requirements under the tax code to protect pass-through corporate taxation. The [IRS guidelines on S corporations](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/s-corporations) dictate that an S corporation cannot have corporate shareholders, partnership shareholders, or multi-member LLC shareholders.

Federal statutory rules permit only individual human beings (who are United States citizens or resident aliens), specific qualifying estates, and certain eligible trusts to hold stock in an S corporation. If an LLC purchases shares in an S corporation, that purchase immediately violates the shareholder eligibility rules. The violation terminates the corporation's S election, automatically reclassifying the business as a standard C corporation subject to corporate income tax.

This fundamental shareholder restriction represents the single biggest practical difference between corporate types when designing multi-entity setups. Business owners comparing pass-through options should examine our [guide on S corp vs C corp differences](/compare/s-corp-vs-c-corp/) to see how shareholder restrictions influence entity planning. A C corporation provides total shareholder flexibility, while an S corporation trades that shareholder flexibility for pass-through tax status.

sections.heading: Corporate Ownership of LLC Subsidiaries
sections.body:
Ownership works equally well in reverse: a C corporation can own an LLC. Under the business entity statutes of all fifty states, any legal person or entity, including a domestic or foreign corporation, is legally permitted to become a member of an LLC. When a C corporation holds one hundred percent of the membership interests in an LLC, the limited liability company functions as a wholly owned subsidiary.

Corporations frequently establish subsidiary LLCs for targeted operational purposes. One primary business reason is liability segregation. A corporation operating multiple lines of business can place a volatile product line, hazardous manufacturing operations, or high-risk commercial real estate into a dedicated LLC subsidiary. If a legal claim, contract default, or slip-and-fall accident occurs at the property owned by the subsidiary LLC, the liabilities remain confined inside that specific limited liability container rather than threatening the parent corporation's primary operating treasury.

Another frequent application is holding intellectual property or ring-fencing discrete enterprise assets. A corporation can hold valuable trademarks, patents, or software code in a specialized LLC subsidiary and license those assets back to parent business units. Additionally, when two independent companies choose to pursue a joint commercial project, they often structure the joint venture by co-owning a newly formed LLC rather than creating complex equity-sharing arrangements inside their core corporate entities.

sections.heading: Tax Mechanics for a Corporation-Owned LLC
sections.body:
The federal tax treatment of an LLC owned entirely by a C corporation depends on the entity classification regulations established by the federal government. Under the Treasury Department's check-the-box regulations, a domestic single-member LLC defaults to being a disregarded entity for federal tax purposes. The [IRS guidelines on limited liability companies](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/limited-liability-company-llc) establish that a disregarded entity has no independent existence for federal corporate income tax assessment.

Because the single-member LLC is treated as a disregarded entity, it does not file a separate federal income tax return. Instead, all gross receipts, costs of goods sold, deductible operational expenses, depreciation allowances, and balance-sheet items flow directly onto the parent C corporation's federal tax return (Form 1120). The tax code treats the activities of the subsidiary LLC as if the parent C corporation had conducted those activities through an internal branch or operating division.

This disregarded classification provides considerable administrative efficiency. A corporate enterprise achieves full state-law liability protection for its distinct subsidiary business operations without adding the complexity of multi-tiered federal corporate tax filings. The corporate parent reports the subsidiary income directly, paying federal corporate income taxes on combined net business income.

sections.heading: Legal Entity Distinctions and Form 8832 Elections
sections.body:
An LLC is not automatically a C corporation, and confusing legal formation with tax classification creates major structural mistakes. An LLC is a legal business entity created under state law by filing articles of organization with a state business registrar. In contrast, a C corporation describes a tax status governed by Subchapter C of Chapter 1 of the Internal Revenue Code. Under default federal tax rules, a single-member LLC is classified as a disregarded entity, while a multi-member LLC is classified as a tax partnership.

An LLC can, however, elect to receive C corporation tax treatment by filing [IRS Form 8832](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8832). When an LLC makes this entity classification election, it instructs the federal government to tax its profits under Subchapter C rules, subjecting the company to federal corporate income tax rates. Detailed requirements for this election appear in our [Form 8832 entity classification guide](/guides/form-8832-entity-classification-election/).

Electing C corporation tax treatment via Form 8832 changes only federal tax administration; it does not alter the underlying state-law legal structure. The business remains an LLC governed by its state operating agreement and LLC statutes. Making this election does not create or issue shares of corporate stock. Membership units remain membership interests, and the entity cannot issue standardized common or preferred share certificates until the owners execute a formal statutory conversion under state corporate law. Business owners seeking a complete corporate structure should read our [guide on converting an LLC to a C corp](/guides/how-to-convert-llc-to-c-corp/).

sections.heading: Holding Companies vs Operating Companies
sections.body:
Deciding whether an LLC should own a C corporation depends heavily on the functional difference between an investment holding vehicle and an active operating enterprise. Using an LLC as a parent holding company is a proven strategy for family offices, angel syndicates, and private investment partnerships. The holding LLC pools capital from multiple members, maintains pass-through partnership tax treatment for its underlying owners, and holds diverse equity assets, including blocks of stock in privately held or publicly traded C corporations.

That holding-company structure is entirely distinct from an active startup seeking institutional investment. Early-stage high-growth technology companies cannot cleanly raise institutional capital while operating as an LLC. Institutional venture capital funds universally require the operating business itself to be formed as a Delaware C corporation rather than an LLC. Institutional funds include tax-exempt investors such as university endowments and pension funds, as well as foreign limited partners. These institutional investors cannot accept pass-through income or unrelated business taxable income (UBTI) generated by an operating LLC.

Furthermore, venture capital firms require standardized preferred stock with specific liquidation preferences, protective provisions, and dividend rights that are native to corporate charters. An investor holding company using an LLC to hold C corporation shares works smoothly, but an operating business attempting to solicit venture funding as an LLC creates tax friction and legal obstacles. Founders choosing between these core paths can evaluate our [LLC vs C corp comparison guide](/compare/llc-vs-c-corp/) to align entity choices with long-term capital plans.

faqItems.question: Can my LLC be a shareholder in a C corporation?
faqItems.answer: Yes, your LLC can be a shareholder in a C corporation. Federal tax law and state corporate statutes place no limitations on who or what entity may hold shares in a C corporation. Your LLC can purchase corporate stock, hold share certificates in the company name, and receive dividend distributions directly into its business bank account.

faqItems.question: Can an LLC own an S corp the same way it can own a C corp?
faqItems.answer: No, an LLC generally cannot hold shares in an S corporation. Federal tax rules restrict S corporation ownership to individuals who are United States citizens or residents, along with specific eligible trusts and estates. If an LLC acquires stock in an S corporation, the business immediately violates S corp eligibility requirements and loses its pass-through tax status, reverting to a C corporation.

faqItems.question: Why would a C corp want to own an LLC instead of just running the business itself?
faqItems.answer: A C corporation forms an LLC subsidiary primarily to isolate legal liabilities and segment distinct commercial assets. By holding real estate, distinct product lines, joint venture operations, or intellectual property inside a separate limited liability company, legal claims or debts arising in that subsidiary remain isolated from the parent corporation's core operating treasury.

faqItems.question: If my LLC elects to be taxed as a C corp, does that mean it can suddenly issue stock?
faqItems.answer: No, electing C corporation tax treatment by filing Form 8832 changes only federal tax classification, not state-law entity mechanics. The business remains an LLC under state law and continues to be owned through membership interests defined by an operating agreement. To issue legal corporate stock certificates, the owners must complete a formal statutory conversion into a state-chartered corporation.
